blocks.text: Biogeography, the study of the geographic distribution of plants and animals, shows that life in different parts of the world has distinctive evolutionary histories.

items: Similar groups of organisms can live in places separated by vast barriers; their similarities suggest common ancestry and their differences millions of years of independent evolution. The book's example is the African lion and the mountain lion of America.

Organisms separated by geographical barriers are often very different despite similar environments; many animals of Australia and Tasmania, where many species of kangaroo are the main herbivores, differ from animals anywhere else.
Islands often have relatively few but unique species, because of colonisation followed by evolution on the island.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Similar groups far apart: two continents separated by ocean, each with a related animal. Different animals in similar places: an outline of Australia and Tasmania, home of unique animals such as kangaroos. Islands: a cluster of islands with few but unique species.
blocks.caption: Three patterns of biogeography (original diagram for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Biogeography, the study of where plants and animals are found, shows that different parts of the world have distinct evolutionary histories. Similar groups living far apart, separated by barriers such as oceans, suggest common ancestry, while their differences reflect millions of years of independent evolution. Areas cut off by geographical barriers, such as Australia and Tasmania, have very different animals even where environments are similar, and islands often have few but unique species, the result of colonisation followed by evolution on the island.

blocks.title: About the lions
blocks.text: The mountain lion (puma or cougar) of the Americas belongs to a different genus from the African lion; both are cats, and their shared features come from the common ancestry of the cat family.

blocks.prompt: Why do islands often have unique species?
blocks.explanation: A few colonists reach the island and then evolve there in isolation, so their descendants become species found nowhere else.

items: Similar groups far apart: common ancestry, independent evolution.
